title: Teacher burnout, the behaviour crisis and the hippocampus: why "I can't think" is a system signal
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes uses the hippocampus - the brain region central to memory formation and stress regulation - to explain why burnout so often feels like 'brain fog' rather than simple tiredness. She connects chronic classroom stress to specific memory tasks teachers rely on daily (remembering pupil needs, source memory for incidents, prospective memory for follow-ups) and cites recent NFER, DfE and NASUWT data linking worsening pupil behaviour directly to workload, wellbeing and retention outcomes. She argues behaviour-related stress is especially toxic because it combines unpredictability, social threat and no recovery loop, and closes with separate practical recommendations for teachers (externalise memory, reduce decision fatigue, protect sleep) and for leaders (make behaviour predictable, reduce chronic load, build planning systems that reduce cognitive burden, protect recovery time).
points: Hughes's central neuroscience framing - linking chronic stress and cortisol to hippocampus-dependent memory tasks - gives a physiological explanation for the common teacher complaint of 'brain fog' during burnout.

She cites a February 2026 NFER analysis linking pupil behaviour and support for disruption directly to teacher retention outcomes, grounding the argument in current UK policy data rather than anecdote alone.

Her three-factor model of why behaviour-related stress is especially toxic - unpredictability, social threat, no recovery loop - gives leaders a precise diagnostic frame distinct from generic 'workload' talk.

She deliberately splits recommendations into what individual teachers can do versus what only leaders can fix, explicitly rejecting the idea that burnout can be solved through individual self-care alone.
quotes: If you ask teachers what burnout feels like, you'll probably hear the same phrase in a hundred variations: brain fog. That experience isn't a personal failure. It's what sustained stress does to the brain systems that support memory, learning, and emotional regulation, especially the hippocampus.

A February 2026 NFER analysis... reports that teachers in schools with good pupil behaviour and support to deal with disruption are more likely to stay. The DfE's National Behaviour Survey reports 73% of teachers said pupil misbehaviour negatively affected their health and wellbeing.

The hippocampus helps map patterns and predict what comes next. But persistent low-level disruption creates an environment where teachers can't reliably anticipate the next interruption. The brain stays alert, which is an exhausting state when it becomes the default.

Burnout is often described as emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation and reduced sense of accomplishment. But behaviour pressures accelerate all three... your professional identity narrows from teacher to crowd controller.
If behaviour is a retention issue, it must be treated as a workplace safety and workload issue, not a character test for teachers.
